en: The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Teaching Regarding the Disturbances Caused by Māra;
the translator’s name is lost, appended to the Later Han Record.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at the Deer Park in Ṛṣipatana, near Vārāṇasī in the country of the Vṛjis.
In the park at that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was constructing a cave for the Blessed One; he was pacing back and forth in the open air, instructing the workers on how to build it.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas transformed his body into something minute and entered the belly of the Venerable Maudgalyāyana.
Then, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"For what reason?"
"My belly has become heavy, as if I had eaten beans; I should enter the samādhi of such an appearance and, with a mind in samādhi, observe my own belly."
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana left the place where he had been pacing to and fro, went to the walking path, spread out his sitting mat, and sat down cross-legged.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered into meditative absorption (*samādhi*) according to its specific form; with his mind in samādhi, he observed his own belly.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately knew: "This Māra Pāpīyān has entered into my belly."
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana arose from his samādhi and addressed Māra Pāpīyas, saying:
"Come out, Pāpīyas! Come out, Pāpīyas!"
"Do not harass the Tathāgata or the disciples of the Tathāgata; do not encounter immeasurable suffering for a long night, which would be without purpose or benefit.
Thereupon, Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa neither knows nor sees, yet he speaks these words:"
"Come out, Pāpīyan! Come out, Pāpīyan!"
"Go! Do not harass the Tathāgata or the disciples of the Tathāgata; do not encounter immeasurable suffering for a long night, which would be harmful and without benefit.
He thought: "If that Blessed One possesses such power and such capability, yet even that Blessed One cannot know me or see me, how much less could his disciples know or see me?"
"This is not so! Pāpīyan, I also know what you are thinking."
You thought to yourself:
"The śramaṇa neither knows nor sees, yet he speaks these words: 'Pāpīyan!'"
Begone! Pāpīyan! Begone!
"Do not provoke or harass the Tathāgata or the disciples of the Tathāgata; do not encounter immeasurable suffering for a long night, which would be meaningless and without benefit.
This is because that Blessed One possesses such power and such capability, yet even he cannot know me or see me, much less could his disciples know or see me?
"This cannot be so! Then Māra Pāpīyān again thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa must have perceived me, for he has spoken these words."
"Come out, Pāpīyan! Come out, Pāpīyan!"
"Come out!
Do not harass the Tathāgata or his disciples; do not encounter immeasurable suffering for a long night, which would be meaningless and unbeneficial.
Thereupon, Māra Pāpīyas emerged from the mouth of the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and stood before him.
After Māra Pāpīyas had withdrawn to stand to one side, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed Pāpīyas, saying: "Pāpīyas!
In the past, in a previous age, there was a Tathāgata named Kakusandha, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
At that time, I was also being harassed by Māra.
I had a sister named Kālī, and you are her son.
You, Pāpīyan!
By this you should know that you are my sister’s daughter.
That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda had a disciple named Vairocanasvara-svāti, who was the most supreme, the most virtuous, and superior to all other disciples.
For what reason, Pāpīyan, do you cause the Venerable Vīra to be called Vīrasena? Pāpīyan!

This Venerable Vīra dwells in the Brahma Heaven and is able to fill a thousand worlds with his voice. Among his disciples, there is none who equals him, none who equals his voice, and none who resembles him in his ability to preach the Dharma.
For this reason, Pāpīyān caused the Venerable Vīra to be named Vīrasena.
By what skillful means did Pāpīyān cause him to be named Sena and given the title Sena?

This one named Śarabha, Pāpīyan, dwells near a village or city; rising early, he puts on his robes, takes up his bowl and outer garment, and enters the village or city to beg for food. He guards his own body, his faculties are fully controlled, and his mind is always settled in meditative concentration.

Having gone to the villages and towns to beg for alms, he returns in the afternoon; he puts away his robes and bowl, washes his feet, takes up his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), and placing it over his right shoulder, he goes to a secluded place, or to the foot of a tree, or to an open space. There, having spread out his sitting mat, he sits cross-legged and, with lightness and swiftness, enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*).

Among them, if a shepherd sees a cowherd, or a woodcutter, or a traveler, and perceives that the latter has quickly entered the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), he thinks upon seeing this:

"This ascetic, sitting in this secluded place, has now passed away. We should take dry grass, wood, or cow dung—or perhaps spread out crushed grass and wood—and pile it over his body; having set fire to it, we shall return."
Then those shepherds, cowherds, wood-gatherers, and travelers spread dry grass and wood, or scattered crushed grass and wood over their bodies, set them on fire, and then departed and returned.
Then, when the night had passed, the Venerable Sāṇa arose from samādhi; he quickly and lightly gathered and smoothed his robes and dwelt near the city village.

Rising at dawn, he put on his garments and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the city village for alms. He was able to guard himself, his faculties were fully mastered, and his mind remained constantly concentrated.
If those shepherds, cowherds, wood-gatherers, or travelers who see him there should think: "This ascetic has passed away in this secluded place;
let us cover his body with dry grass, wood, and cow dung, or by spreading out crushed grass and wood, pile them over him, set fire to it, and then depart," [he would be reborn in such a state].
"Now this Venerable One has returned and his life still endures.
Because of this expedient means, Pāpīyān is named Sarva, and his title is Sarva-āpanna (Sarva-returning-to-life).
Then, Dūsī, Pāṭika, and Kharaka thought to themselves:
"This shaven-headed śramaṇa has black wrapped around his body; he dwells together with dhyāna, is associated with dhyāna, and constantly practices dhyāna."

It is like a donkey constantly carrying a load, tethered to a manger; though it may not receive barley, it meditates and meditates, remains associated with meditation, and constantly practices meditation.
Thus, this shaven-headed śramaṇa, with his body wrapped in black robes, dwells together with dhyāna, is associated with dhyāna, and practices dhyāna.
He is like a kitten sitting before a mouse hole, desiring to catch the mouse within; he meditates, is associated with dhyāna, and practices dhyāna.
Thus, this shaven-headed śramaṇa, with his body wrapped in black robes, is constantly accompanied by dhyāna, conjoined with dhyāna, and always practices dhyāna.
He is just like an owl or a fox on a ruined wall, catching mice therein; he meditates and meditates, conjoined with dhyāna, and always practices dhyāna.
In this way, this shaven-headed śramaṇa, with his body wrapped in black, constantly dwells together with dhyāna, is associated with dhyāna, and always practices dhyāna.
He is like a cormorant on the riverbank, watching for fish within the water, absorbed in dhyāna after dhyāna.
Thus, this shaven-headed śramaṇa, with his body wrapped in black, is in accord with dhyāna; he meditates, truly meditating.
What is this called "dhyāna"?
For what purpose does he meditate?
"What kind of meditation is this?

It is either distracted, forgetful, or unsettled; I do not see it coming, nor do I see it going, nor do I see it staying, nor do I see its end, nor do I see its arising. I should indeed explain this to the brahmins and householders."
In this way, one should revile this ascetic, strike him, speak ill of him, and show him anger; whether it be a little or much, one should revile, strike, and with resentment speak of his faults.
"If there is any lapse in his mind, this evil Māra will seek an opportunity, look for an opening; he may find that opportunity, or find the causal conditions for it.
Thus, this Māra Pāpīyān, acting as an evil demon, said to the brahmins and householders:
"That śramaṇa is practicing with diligence; you should revile him, speak of his faults, and direct anger toward him."
They shall strike that diligent śramaṇa with wood, hurl stones at him, or lash him with a staff; they shall even split his head open, tear his robes, or break his bowl.

That is to say, at that time, those brahmins and householders, having passed away due to those causes and conditions, with the breakup of the body after death, were reborn in the miserable states, in the hells.
Having been born there, they thought:
"Now we have already experienced this suffering; perhaps there may be even more intense suffering than this place, yet we directed our minds toward wrong views regarding the diligent śramaṇas."

"Then Pāpīyān took disciples of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krukusunda, broke their heads, shattered their bowls, and tore their robes; he then went before the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krukusunda."
"At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda was surrounded by an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands, and was preaching the Dharma for them."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda saw from afar his disciple approaching, his head shattered and his robes and bowl torn.
Having seen this, he addressed the bhikṣus: "O bhikṣus!
You should see this bhikṣu, who acts as a wretched Māra, speaking to the brahmins and householders thus:"
“You should take up a vigorous śramaṇa, revile him, and strike him; you should strike him with some degree of anger, for perhaps through such an angry mind, there may arise some [realization].”
And this wretched Māra sought an opportunity and sought the causal conditions; having sought the causal conditions, he found them.
You, O bhikṣus!

Having first dwelt in meditative absorption, pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he likewise pervades the second, third, and fourth directions, as well as above, below, and across—all quarters of space—with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; free from enmity, free from duality, and free from ill will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and thoroughly developed, he dwells in meditative absorption, pervading all quarters of space.

In this way, with his mind accompanied by compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, having suffused all directions, he dwells in right attainment; thus, even if Māra the Evil One seeks an opportunity or searches for a causal condition, he shall find no opportunity and find no causal condition.
Thereupon, Pāpīyas addressed the disciples of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda, saying these words:

"He dwells having attained meditative absorption, suffusing one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, above, below, and across—all quarters of space—with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, free from enmity, free from duality, and free from ill will; vast, exalted, immeasurable, and perfectly purified, he dwells having attained meditative absorption, suffusing all directions."
In this way, with his mind accompanied by compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, he dwells having attained meditative absorption that pervades all directions.
Thus, when that evil Māra seeks an opportunity and searches for a causal condition, he cannot find such an opportunity, nor can he find such a causal condition.
Thereupon, Pāpīyān Māra thought to himself:
"By these means, I cannot find an opportunity against this śramaṇa; I cannot find the causal conditions to overcome him. I would rather go to the brahmins and householders and say:
'You should take up this diligent śramaṇa and respectfully serve, honor, revere, and make offerings to him.'"

After having made some small measure of offerings, service, and veneration, if his mind becomes distracted, that evil Māra will seek an opportunity, seek an opening, and seek the causal conditions; he will find that opportunity and find those causal conditions.
"This evil Māra Pāpīyas says to the householders and brahmins:
'That diligent śramaṇa should be honored, served, and revered.'"
He then had the brahmins and householders strip off their garments and spread them upon the ground, saying:
"Let this diligent śramaṇa tread upon these; let the diligent śramaṇa travel upon these."
"This ascetic of diligence practices such extreme austerities that he shall surely bring us benefit and welfare for a long night.
He then had the brahmins and householders wash their own hair and spread it upon the ground, saying:
"Ascetic of diligence!..."
You should practice the higher path,
O diligent śramaṇa!
You should wander in the higher path.
"This ascetic is practicing extreme austerities; may he bring us benefit and welfare for a long night.
Then, they should cause the brahmins and householders to hold bags filled with various things in their hands and say these words:
"May you, O worthy ones, please [accept this]!"
"You should take this as you see fit;
may it bring us long-term benefit and welfare.
To inspire faith and devotion in the brahmins and householders, he personally took hold of those diligent śramaṇas with his own hand, led them into his home, and offered whatever they desired.
"May the worthy ones please accept this gift and use it as they see fit; may we thereby obtain long-term benefit and welfare.

At that time, those brahmins and householders passed away. On account of that cause and condition, at the breaking up of the body after death, they were reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly realms. Having been reborn there, they then had this thought:
"We have no pleasure greater than this, because we have directed ourselves toward the śramaṇa who possesses right view.

Thereupon, Pāpīyas, having made offerings, paid respect, served, and honored the disciples of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda, went to where those disciples of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda were.
"At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda was surrounded by an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands who stood before him as he preached the Dharma."
The Tathāgata Krakucchanda, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, saw from afar his disciple coming from a distance, having been honored, revered, served, and venerated by others.
Having seen him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see this, bhikṣus?
This is the wretched Māra Pāpīyān!"
He said to the brahmins and householders:
"One should provide offerings, show respect, serve, and pay homage to that diligent śramaṇa with reverence.

If one’s mind wavers while providing even a small amount of reverence, service, homage, and offerings, then that evil Māra Pāpīyān will seek an opportunity and look for a cause; he will find his opportunity and find his cause."

"O monks! You should view all conditioned phenomena as lacking permanence; you should view them as subject to exhaustion, as subject to detachment, as subject to cessation, as subject to stilling, and as having a state of rest."
"And yet, although the evil Māra Pāpīyas seeks an opportunity and looks for a cause, he finds no opportunity and finds no cause.
Then that Pāpīyas spoke these words to the disciples of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krukusanda:
"In all these conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras), one sees their impermanence, their exhaustion, their detachment, their cessation, and their state of stillness."
"That evil Māra Pāpīyān sought an opportunity and searched for a causal condition, but he could not find an opportunity nor obtain a causal condition.
Then the evil Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"By this means, I have been unable to find an opportunity against this diligent śramaṇa, nor have I obtained a causal condition."
"I would rather transform myself into the form of a young boy and stand by his path.
Holding a large piece of wood in my hand, I shall strike the Venerable Viśvāmitra with it, breaking him so that blood flows."

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krukusunda resided in a town and village. Rising early in the morning, he put on his robes, took up his bowl and outer robe, and intended to enter the town and village for alms, accompanied by the Venerable Vīra and a following of bhikṣus.

Thereupon, the Wicked Māra, having manifested himself in another place in the form of a young boy, stood by the side of the road holding a large piece of wood in his hand and struck the Venerable Pilindavatsa, causing blood to flow.
Thereupon, the Venerable Virūḍhaka was struck; his head was split open and blood flowed as he followed behind the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda.

Then, having arrived at the village, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kruḷūna, with the full strength of his entire body, turned his gaze to the right in a circumambulatory manner; without fear, without terror, without alarm, and without trepidation, he surveyed all directions.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda saw the Venerable Virūḍhaka being struck, his head shattered and blood flowing, as he approached from behind; having seen this, he said:
"This wretched Māra acts wrongly; he knows no contentment."
"Furthermore, Pāpīyan!
Before the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda had even finished speaking these words, at that moment the wicked Māra fell with his very body into the great hell."
That Pāpīyān, within the great niraya hell, possesses four conditions and lacks the pleasure of the six sense-contact bases; his body currently undergoes agony, fettered by chains of linked hooks.
It means that the hell-wardens of that hell go to the presence of Māra, the Evil One; having arrived, they speak thus:
"If these shackles of yours are released, you should know that I have been in hell for a full hundred years."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas was so terrified that the hair on his body stood on end.
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately spoke this verse:
"How can you dwell in hell, and yet allow evil to reside within?"
One who offends a Buddha or a brahmin, And one who offends this bhikṣu,
Is said to be in the Avīci hell, Causing evil to cease within it;
One who offends a Buddha or a brahmin, And one who offends this bhikṣu.
When the fetters are loosened, one becomes a hundredfold;
suffering and pain abide within, in the Avīci hell, causing evil to dwell therein.
If there are those who do not know this, they are but monks who are disciples of the Buddha.
Experiencing suffering such as this, one shall receive the retribution of black karma.
Whether dwelling in pleasure groves or among the beings of this earth,
those who do not plant and cultivate rice shall be reborn in Uttarakuru.
The vast Mount Sumeru approaches liberation;
those who can discern for themselves maintain mindfulness in their conduct.
That mountain rests within the spring, abiding eternally throughout this kalpa.
His form is like the color of gold, and his radiance shines everywhere.
He performs various kinds of music; this is where Śakra’s music dwells.
There too are two [attendants] who stand before him in reverence.
If a Śākya goes before them, they ascend this lofty hall;
seeing from where the Śākya comes, each finds their own delight.
But if they see a bhikṣu coming, they turn back in shame.
If there should be one who ascends the hall and is able to question the bhikṣu, know that such a Māra exists;
yet through the exhaustion of craving, one attains liberation.
This bhikṣu should be declared thus: "Upon hearing this teaching, it should be understood in this way."
"Kauśika, I know you; having exhausted craving, you have attained liberation.
Hearing this declaration of wisdom, Śakra has obtained joy and happiness.
O bhikṣu who has performed much practice, I shall further explain this for you."
If there is one who ascends this hall, O Śākyan, you are able to pose a question:
"What is meant by 'hall,' and why do you, O Śākyan, stand upon it?
O Śākyan, I shall explain to you: this is called the place where retribution is received.
Within such a thousandfold world system, there exists this thousandfold world;
no hall surpasses this, nor any such place for receiving retribution.
Śakra moves with sovereign ease, most luminous and pure among them all.
Transforming one into a hundred, he dwells here upon the Hall of Retribution;
attaining liberation, he wanders with ease, ascending this hall where he can move it with his toe,
causing those with the divine eye to behold him.
The Śākya attained mastery and wanders freely, ascending upon the Deer Park terrace.
With supernormal powers he can move and transform; it is profoundly deep and utterly concealed.
Difficult to shake and difficult to turn, there lies a floor of lapis lazuli.
The dwelling place of the Sage is smooth and exceedingly soft;
the mats spread thereon are most supple, and his speech is likewise gentle.
This most excellent Deva King is well-able to perform music.
Various and manifold, diverse are the devas who have gathered in assembly;
those tending toward the stage of stream-entry (srotāpanna) number in the thousands and tens of millions,
reaching as far as the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa).
The teaching of the Dharma acts as an eye;
having heard this Dharma, one who believes and delights in it is indeed acceptable.
Knowing that such a Dharma exists, he is called a seer (ṛṣi), and is said to have reached the Brahma-heaven.
When the various Brahmās asked me, "Does that Brahmā hold this view?"—the view he held was as previously described: "He always perceives existence as permanent.
I then gave my prediction to the Brahmās: "O Seer, regarding this view of mine,"
Not seeing it as it was before, I always maintain that there is permanence.
Seeing the correspondence of my retribution, the body of Brahmā appears before me;
what should I say now? I constantly reckon that there is permanence.
It is said that one who understands this world, as taught by the Fully Awakened One, will experience the retribution for whatever they have cultivated.
Fire has no such thought: "I shall burn the foolish person."
When fire has already burned a fool, it continues to burn him as he walks away.
So it is with you, Pāpīyas: having long committed such evil deeds in the presence of this Tathāgata, you shall likewise experience their retribution for a long time.
"You, Māra, do not weary of the Buddha, nor do you harass the bhikṣu;
for this bhikṣu speaks thus, and Māra is in the country of Nāsya.
The ghost has thoughts of sorrow and grief, moved by the diligent efforts of Maudgalyāyana."
Terror and extreme dread suddenly vanish;
thus spoke the Buddha in the *Māraparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
